scenes.narration: Eleven billion dollars. That is what the United States government says its gold is worth, on its own official books.

But at the market price of gold at the end of September twenty twenty-five, the very same gold was worth, by our calculation, about one trillion dollars. Nearly a hundred times more. Same bars, same vaults.

keyframes.cue: the very same gold was worth
keyframes.label: items[2].at.cue

scenes.narration: So why does the world's biggest economy still value its gold like it is nineteen seventy-three?

By the end of this video, you will know where that gold really sits, why it still carries a price from the seventies, who checks that it is really there, and what could happen if someone rewrote the price.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Start with the pile itself. According to the Treasury, the government owns about two hundred and sixty-one million ounces of gold. By our calculation, that is about eight thousand one hundred tonnes. And the number has barely moved in decades. A congressional audit office counted almost exactly the same amount in twenty ten.

Most of it is not where you might think. Fort Knox, in Kentucky, holds about fifty-six percent. West Point, in New York, about twenty-one percent. The Mint in Denver, about seventeen percent. And about five percent sits in a vault under the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

keyframes.cue: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
keyframes.label: items[0].bars[3].at.cue

scenes.narration: Almost all of it sits in what the Mint calls deep storage, sealed vaults that are not touched for daily work. The Treasury's inspector general notes that the Mint did not use any of that deep storage gold to make coins in twenty twenty-four or twenty twenty-five. The gold is not inventory. It is a reserve that simply sits there, year after year.

The New York slice is small, but not trivial. Inspectors counted about thirteen and a half million ounces held by the Federal Reserve Banks, almost all of it in the New York vault. At the market price of September twenty twenty-five, that slice alone was worth about fifty-one billion dollars, more than four times the official value of all the gold combined.

Here is a detail that surprises a lot of people. The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, does not own any of this gold. In its own words, the Federal Reserve does not own gold. The owner is the Treasury. The Fed only holds a small part of it for safekeeping.

Let me draw where the gold sits. Here is the whole stack, two hundred and sixty-one million ounces. Fort Knox takes the biggest bar. Then West Point. Then Denver. And a thin slice in New York. More than half of America's gold sits behind one set of doors in Kentucky.

keyframes.cue: a thin slice in New York

scenes.narration: So the gold is real, and it is enormous. The strange part is the price written next to it.

keyframes.label: The gold is real, and enormous…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: For a long time, the dollar was defined in gold. From nineteen hundred, an ounce was worth twenty dollars and sixty-seven cents. In nineteen thirty-four, the government raised it to thirty-five dollars an ounce. That one change cut the gold value of the dollar to about fifty-nine percent of what it had been.

Then came two laws in quick succession. In March nineteen seventy-two, Congress set the price at thirty-eight dollars. And in September nineteen seventy-three, it raised it one last time, to forty-two and two-ninths dollars. That is forty-two dollars and twenty-two cents an ounce. The same law also started to end the ban on Americans owning gold.

And then, nothing. The market price of gold went its own way, but the official price never moved again. It is still written into federal law today. Every ounce in Fort Knox is booked at forty-two dollars and twenty-two cents.

Let me draw two prices on the same chart. The official price climbs in small steps, then goes flat after nineteen seventy-three. The market price leaves it behind. At the end of September twenty twenty-five, the market paid about three thousand eight hundred and twenty-five dollars an ounce. By our calculation, that is about ninety times the official price.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Why would anyone keep such an old number? Because that number is not just a label. It is tied to real money at the central bank.

keyframes.label: Why keep such an old number?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In nineteen thirty-four, the Gold Reserve Act made the Federal Reserve hand all its gold to the Treasury. In return, the Fed received gold certificates. They are written in dollars, and they cannot be swapped back for gold.

The Congressional Research Service explains the trick. The Treasury monetized the gold by issuing those certificates to the Fed, and the Fed put the money into the Treasury's own bank account. But there is a limit. The certificates can never be worth more than the gold's official value.

That is why the numbers match so closely. The Federal Reserve's weekly balance sheet shows a gold stock of about eleven billion dollars, and a gold certificate account of eleven point oh three seven billion dollars. The gold has already been turned into money, at the nineteen seventy-three price.

Let me draw the loop. Here is the Treasury, with the gold. Here is the Federal Reserve. The Treasury sends certificates to the Fed. The Fed sends dollars back into the Treasury's account. The gold itself never moves. Only the paper and the money do.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Of course, all of this only works if the gold is really there. So who checks?

keyframes.label: It only works if the gold is there…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In nineteen seventy-four, after questions in Congress, the Government Accountability Office helped plan an audit of Fort Knox. Auditors checked three of the thirteen vault compartments, and found no differences. The next year, the Treasury set up a permanent committee to keep auditing the gold.

By nineteen eighty-six, about ninety-two percent of the gold had been audited. And since nineteen ninety-five, the Treasury's inspector general has audited the gold in deep storage every single year, checking the seals on all forty-two compartments. Its latest report gave the Mint a clean opinion.

Official visits make the news. In August twenty seventeen, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin flew to Fort Knox with Senate leader Mitch McConnell. The trip fell on the day of a solar eclipse, and the inspector general looked into it. It found no indication that the date was chosen for the eclipse. The plane cost about twenty-six thousand nine hundred dollars.

Some lawmakers still want more. In twenty twenty-five, a House bill proposed a full independent audit of all the gold, every five years. It is a proposal. As far as the official record we could check, it has not become law.

Let me draw the vault. Forty-two compartments, each one sealed. Every year, inspectors check the seals. Once in a while, a compartment is opened and the bars are counted and tested. Trust, but verify, one door at a time.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Which brings us to the most tempting idea of all. What if the government simply updated the price?

keyframes.label: The most tempting idea of all…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: On paper, the gap is huge. Booked at the market price of September twenty twenty-five, the gold would jump from about eleven billion dollars to about one trillion. The Congressional Research Service notes that changing the official value would monetize or demonetize gold through those certificates at the Fed.

Some proposals go further. A Senate bill introduced in twenty twenty-five, the BITCOIN Act, would have the Treasury issue new gold certificates at fair market value, partly to help fund a national bitcoin reserve. Again, a proposal, not law.

Here is the catch. Revaluing the gold does not create a single new ounce. It changes a number on a page, and lets the government turn that number into fresh money at the central bank. Supporters see a hidden asset. Critics see printing money with extra steps. Either way, the gold in Kentucky stays exactly where it is.

And it is a lot of gold. According to World Gold Council figures, based on IMF data, China holds around two thousand three hundred and eighty-seven tonnes, and Russia about two thousand two hundred and seventy. By our calculation, the United States holds about three point four times as much as China.

And other countries are still buying. According to the World Gold Council, central banks around the world bought about one hundred and seventy tonnes in the first eight months of twenty twenty-six, with Poland alone adding ninety-eight tonnes. America's own total has barely changed since at least twenty ten. It simply keeps the pile, and keeps the old price.

Let me draw the two balance sheets. On the left, the gold at forty-two dollars, a small brick. On the right, the same gold at the market price, a tower. The bars are identical. Only the price tag changed.

keyframes.cue: Let me draw the two balance sheets
keyframes.label: strokes[0].start.cue

scenes.narration: So why is America's trillion dollars of gold booked at eleven billion? Because a price written into law in nineteen seventy-three still sets how much money that gold can be turned into. The gold is real, it is audited, and it barely moves. The only thing that is out of date is the price tag. And whoever gets to rewrite it gets to create a lot of money.
